newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African parliament endorses agriculture bill.
newsitem.headline: S.African parliament endorses agriculture bill.

text.p: The South African parliament on Wednesday signalled the end of single-channel agricultural marketing, long the backbone of white commercial domination of the industry.
"The days of single channel marketing, fixed prices and control-board domination are over," Agriculture Minister Derek Hanekom told the National Assembly.

"For too long, the statutory marginalisation of marketing opportunities for small farmers was allowed to exist. The legislation before you will finally bring an end to this untenable situation," he said.

The Marketing of Agricultural Products Bill won unanimous support, though several parties expressed reservations about some provisions or about the reluctance of the ruling African National Congress to consider amendments.
"We support this bill, but with great reservations and concern," said National Party farming spokesman Isak van Zyl.
"Please make sure that we do not have the same hasty and faulty application of corrective measures in agriculture that we have seen elsewhere. That would be fatal," he said.
The bill, likely to be implemented next year, provides for a National Agricultural Marketing Council to advise the minister on measures to promote or protect the industry.

It sets a 13-month timetable for the dismantling of remaining control boards that dominate the production and marketing of commodities including fruit, cotton, maize, meat, mohair, lucerne, wheat, oilseeds and wool.
Any future intervention would have to be in consultation with each of five "directly affected groups" defined in the bill as producers, including labour, vendors, buyers, processors and consumers.
Interventions could take the form of a levy of up to five percent of the producer's profit, an export control mechanism, pools, obligatory record keeping or a register of producers.
Any measure approved would have to meet one of the following four aims without undermining any of the others:
- Increasing market access for all market participants;
- Improved efficiency of agricultural marketing;
- Optimisation of agricultural export earnings;
- Enhanced viability of the agricultural sector.
The bill also prohibits any measure that would undermine national food security, fair labour practice or the overall number of jobs in the economy.
"The bill is as much about managing transition to deregulated markets as it is about providing for future market interventions," Hanekom said.
He promised also to tackle concentrations that give particular groups domination of export, storage or other facilities.

"It is important that we take steps to ensure a level domestic playing field. It is my intention to do whatever I can to ensure that the agricultural sector operates efficiently to the benefit of all," Hanekom said.
The bill will be put to the vote later this week.
